chunks.title: anti-dive-anti-squat — Anti-dive and anti-squat (side-view geometry)
chunks.excerpt: **Keys:** `under_lower_arm_shims_ff`, `under_lower_arm_shims_fr`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rf`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rr` — the **split** between the forward and rearward inner pickups on one axle (FF−FR front, RF−RR rear) tilts the lower arm's **inner hinge line in side view**. That inclination is the anti-geometry control. The **averaged** stack height on an axle is a separate mechanism — **roll centre / support** on that end (see **support-lower-inner** and **roll-centre**)

chunks.title: anti-dive-anti-squat — Mechanism — wheel path under compression
chunks.excerpt:
Tilting the inner hinge line changes the direction the wheel travels (relative to the chassis) as the suspension compresses. Sign mapping confirmed for this sheet convention:

- **Rear, anti-squat:** hinge inclined so the wheel **sweeps rearward** as it compresses. On throttle, the forward drive force at the contact patch then works **against** compression — the rear squats less. **Raising the forward pickup of the rear arm (RF−RR more positive) = more anti-squat.**
- **Fr

chunks.title: anti-dive-anti-squat — Handling tendencies
chunks.excerpt:
**More rear anti-squat:**

- **Less squat on throttle** — the rear ride height holds up, keeping the front loaded longer, which often reads as **more steering on power** / less exit push.
- Drive force is partly reacted through the links, which can add **initial forward-drive feel** on corner exit.
- The trade: the rear can become **busier over bumps under power** — the same geometry that resists squat also makes drive force fight bump compliance. On rough or low-grip sur

chunks.title: anti-dive-anti-squat — Where it sits among the levers
chunks.excerpt: Anti-geometries act through **longitudinal** force — strongest under braking (entry) and throttle (exit). In real racing the car is almost never in pure steady-state cornering — some brake or throttle is nearly always present — so the influence **blends through the whole corner** rather than switching off mid-corner; only the idealized zero-throttle steady state is (nearly) untouched. Complementary to springs and damper oil, which shape pitch **rate** at all times (see **spri

chunks.title: arb — Anti-roll bar (ARB / sway bar)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `arb_front`, `arb_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-stiffness]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** An ARB is a **bar linking the left and right wheels** at one end of the car. It only
twists when the two wheels move **differently** — that is, in **roll** — so a stiffer bar resists roll
more at that end. When both wheels move **together** (**heave** — a crest, or a bump under both) the bar
just swings and does nothing. So it changes that end's share of roll stiffness without touc

chunks.title: balance-and-grip — Grip, load transfer, and balance
chunks.excerpt:
**Grip** is limited by how much **lateral (or longitudinal) force** each tire can produce. **Load transfer** moves vertical load between tires; **unequally loaded tires** cannot add force in proportion to load at every instant, so the axle’s **usable** grip depends on how load is shared.

**Suspension and geometry stiffness** (roll stiffness, anti geometry, chassis flex where relevant) set how **fast** load moves when the driver steers or the car rolls: **stiffer** paths us

chunks.title: balance-and-grip — Response versus sustained grip
chunks.excerpt:
**Response** here means **lateral bite tied to quick load transfer** right after a steering input or as roll starts: the car **reacts** soon, with a **strong early peak** of side force if the tire and geometry allow it.

**Sustained grip** here means **lateral force that holds later** in the same corner maneuver—through mid-corner roll and steady curvature—often with a **smoother**, **more rolled-in** feel at the limit.

**Stiffer** roll control (springs, ARBs, geometry t

chunks.title: balance-and-grip — Mid-corner understeer
chunks.excerpt:
First separate **corner type** and **phase**: **hairpin / low-speed** vs **high-speed**, and whether the problem is truly **mid-corner** or partly **lack of response on entry** that the driver **reads** as push through the whole corner.

**Hairpins — sustained front limit:** If the front **stops building steering** mid-corner after a reasonable turn-in, the front may lack **sustained grip** relative to what the corner asks—often linked to the front being **too stiff** in ro

chunks.title: balance-and-grip — High-speed understeer and aero
chunks.excerpt:
At **high sustained lateral** load, **aero balance** matters strongly: if the **front aero** is weak **relative to the rear** for the speed and wing setup, the car can feel as if **mechanical balance changes barely move** the push—**more front downforce relative to the rear** (within rules and practicality) is often required for **more high-speed steering**, not only softer front springs.

**Damping** and **nose pitch** still matter (keeping the front loaded in long corners

chunks.title: bump-steer-toe-gain — Bump steer (front)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `bump_steer_shims_front`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Sets how **front toe changes through travel** — the toe-link angle decides whether a wheel
gains toe-in or toe-out as it compresses (and the reverse on extension); shims change that angle. It's
[[toe-and-scrub]] made dynamic: the loaded (compressed) front runs a different toe than its static
value. Shim count isn't a fixed number — measure toe at ride height vs full compression.

chunks.title: bump-steer-toe-gain — Toe gain (rear)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `toe_gain_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]]

**Physics.** The rear version of the same mechanism: the toe-link angle sets how **rear toe changes
through travel**, so the loaded (compressed) outer rear runs a different toe than static. Shims set the
curve, not the static toe.

chunks.title: camber — Camber
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `camber_front`, `camber_rear`
**Concepts:** [[camber-grip]], [[camber-gain]]

**Physics.** Camber is the **tilt** of the tyre relative to the road. More **negative** camber tilts the
top of the tyre inward, helping the **outside** tyre stay nearer flat as the car rolls. The tyre runs
its **static** camber plus [[camber-gain]] in roll; what that effective tilt does to grip is [[camber-grip]].

chunks.title: caster — Front caster
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `caster_front`
**Concepts:** [[camber-grip]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Front caster tilts the **steering axis** back, so the contact patch trails behind where that
axis meets the ground (**mechanical trail**). Two things follow as you steer: the front wheel **gains
camber** (leaning into the corner — feeds [[camber-grip]]), and cornering force acting on the trail
creates a **self-aligning torque** that centres the steering. Most of caster's effect shows up **with

chunks.title: caster — Rear caster
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `caster_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]]

**Physics.** Rear caster acts partly like a small **wheelbase** change (shifts the effective fore-aft
distance between the contact patches) and **interacts with rear toe through travel** — change it and the
rear toe-gain curve ([[toe-and-scrub]]) usually needs re-trimming to match.

chunks.title: damper-oil — Damper oil (thicker vs lighter)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `damper_oil_front`, `damper_oil_rear`
**Concepts:** [[damping]], [[bite-hold]], [[oil-viscosity-temperature]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** Thicker oil raises the **damping force** for a given shaft speed (pistons and holes shape
the curve); lighter lowers it. It's the main knob that sets how much [[damping]] you have.

chunks.title: diff-and-driveline — Differential (rear gear diff)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `diff_oil`
**Concepts:** [[differential-coupling]]

**Physics.** Thicker diff oil raises the diff's **coupling** — it resists a speed difference between the
rear wheels more strongly; thinner frees it. (Ball-diff tightness, one-ways, and a spool are other ways
to set coupling on cars that use them.)

chunks.title: diff-and-driveline — Front driveline (spool) — context, not a lever
chunks.excerpt:
Touring cars run a **spool** front: both front wheels locked to one speed, no coupling knob. It
interacts with steering because steering asks the front wheels for *different* speeds while the spool
forbids it — see steering-geometry-ackermann.

chunks.title: droop-downstop — Droop and downstop (extension travel)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `droop_front`, `droop_rear`, `downstop_front`, `downstop_rear`
**Concepts:** [[bump-compliance]], [[load-transfer]]

**Physics.** Droop/downstop set how far a wheel can **extend** before it hits its **limit**. More
extension lets the wheel reach down to keep **contact** over bumps and as the car rolls; run out of it
and the wheel **tops out** — it can't extend further, so from there that corner goes rigid in droop and
load transfers through a stiff path. Sheets diff

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Flex (general)
chunks.excerpt: **More flex** usually makes the car **more forgiving** and can feel like **more overall grip**, especially when **track grip is low**. When **grip is high**, **too much flex** can feel like **less grip**: **vague**, lacking **support** and **precision**. Flex interacts with **springs, dampers, and geometry** — treat changes as part of a **whole car** balance.

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Front vs rear flex (handling)
chunks.excerpt: **More front flex** tends to **calm initial steering** / feel **smoother on turn-in**, and can add **mid-corner steering** as the nose loads. **More rear flex** often **increases rotation**, especially **on throttle**. **Less rear flex** often **improves rear grip** and **reduces rotation** — but if the rear is **too stiff**, some drivers feel **more rotation on throttle** (unload / snap) depending on diff, springs, and surface. **Test on track.**

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Chassis material (carbon vs steel vs RAF)
chunks.excerpt:
**Key:** `chassis` — options vary by kit (e.g. carbon, steel, RAF-style plates).

**Carbon** is usually the **softest** chassis flavour: often the **most overall grip** in **low-grip** conditions and can be the **easiest** when grip is **low** or the surface is **bumpy / inconsistent**. **Steel** typically **lowers CoG** and has **less flex** than carbon; drivers often use **softer top decks** or other flex tools to **reintroduce** compliance. **RAF / stiff alloy-type** pla

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Top deck: C127 vs C127S (example)
chunks.excerpt: **Keys:** `top_deck_front`, `top_deck_rear` — common presets include **C127** and **C127S** (names from setup sheets). **C127** is often **slightly wider** and therefore **stiffer** than **C127S** in many kits; use your **manual** for the exact part you run.

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Top deck screws and motor mount screws (stiffness)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `top_deck_screws`, `motor_mount_screws` — more screws engaged usually means **more stiffness** in that zone.

- **Top deck screws A–B** (front pair): adding screws here typically adds **front** stiffness.
- **Top deck screws E–F** (rear pair): adding screws here typically adds **rear** stiffness.
- **Motor mount screws** positions **1–2**: often associated with **front** stiffness; positions **3–4–5** with **rear** stiffness (layout is kit-specific — match label

chunks.title: flex-chassis — Top deck cuts (flex)
chunks.excerpt:
**Key:** `top_deck_cuts` — cuts usually **add flex** in the region of the deck.

- Cuts **A–D** (front half of the deck grid): usually **front flex**.
- Cuts **E–H** (rear half): usually **rear flex**.

Use the **same A–H grid** your PDF / app uses; do not assume letters match another brand’s deck.

chunks.title: ride-height-and-rake — Ride height (overall)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `ride_height_front`, `ride_height_rear` — measured chassis-to-ground at defined points, set with the car in race trim.

Ride height sets **CoG height**, and CoG height scales **every load transfer** in the car — lateral (roll), longitudinal (pitch), all of it. **Lower** ride height means **less load transfer** for the same cornering force, which keeps the tire pair on an axle more evenly loaded — **often** more total grip and a more planted platform, but **not alw

chunks.title: ride-height-and-rake — Rake (front vs rear ride height)
chunks.excerpt:
**Rake** = the front/rear ride-height difference. It biases both **static attitude** and how the geometry sits at each end:

- **Rear higher than front (nose-down rake)** tends toward **more steering** — the front carries slightly more static load share, the CoG tips forward, and the rear's higher stance shifts its geometry in travel. Commonly reads as more **turn-in and mid-corner front** at the cost of some **rear security**.
- **Front higher than rear** is the mirror: t

chunks.title: ride-height-and-rake — How to reason about a ride-height question
chunks.excerpt: Separate the three effects before recommending: (1) **CoG / load transfer** (both ends), (2) **geometry shift** at the changed end (camber, roll centre), (3) **rake** (balance). A one-end change is always also a rake change — read it as a balance move, not just a height move.

chunks.title: spring-rate — Spring rate
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `spring_front`, `spring_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-stiffness]], [[bite-hold]], [[motion-ratio]], [[tyre-load-sensitivity]], [[bump-compliance]]

**Physics.** A higher spring rate resists both **heave** (both wheels together) and **roll** more at
that end, and lets that end take load **faster** (it rolls less, so load arrives sooner).

chunks.title: steering-geometry-ackermann — Ackermann (steering-link position)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `inner_steering_angle`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** In a corner the **inside** front runs a **tighter** radius, so it needs **more** steering
angle. Ackermann sets how inner vs outer angles develop as you steer: **more ackermann** points each
front closer to its own arc; **less** (toward parallel) makes them take up more similar angles, loading
the pair harder — [[toe-and-scrub]] across steering, not travel.

chunks.title: steering-geometry-ackermann — Steering throw
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `steer_travel_out`
**Concepts:** [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Caps the **maximum** steering angle — more throw = tighter minimum radius but coarser
proportional control. It doesn't change the ackermann relationship, only how much of it you can reach.

chunks.title: toe — Toe (front & rear)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `toe_front`, `toe_rear`
**Concepts:** [[toe-and-scrub]], [[bite-hold]]

**Physics.** Sets the **static** toe at each end — how far the wheels point in or out at ride height.
Touring fronts are often run **toe-out**, rears **toe-in**; what toe does to the tyre is [[toe-and-scrub]].
Sheet signs differ — confirm whether a bigger number means more toe-in or toe-out before comparing.

chunks.title: under-hub — Under-hub shims (axle height / outer lower)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `under_hub_shims_front`, `under_hub_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]]

**Physics.** Adding shims under the hub pushes the **outer** end of the lower arm down — further from
the hub — flattening the lower arm, which **raises the roll centre** on that corner. Removing shims
does the reverse. A pure RC move — it adds nothing beyond roll centre.

**Effects (context-dependent — confirm on track).**
- All of them are that roll-centre change working through [[roll-

chunks.title: under-lower-arm — Under-lower-arm shims (inner lower pickup)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `under_lower_arm_shims_ff`, `under_lower_arm_shims_fr`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rf`, `under_lower_arm_shims_rr`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]]

**Physics.** Adding shims under the inner end of the lower arm raises that pickup, tilting the lower
arm — which **raises the roll centre** on that corner. It is the **strongest single lever on roll
centre** (far more RC per shim than the upper link or the hub), and it moves RC and camber gain
together in the same direction.

chunks.title: upper-link-geometry — Upper-link geometry (inner + outer shims)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `upper_inner_shims_ff`, `upper_inner_shims_fr`, `upper_inner_shims_rf`, `upper_inner_shims_rr`, `upper_outer_shims_front`, `upper_outer_shims_rear`
**Concepts:** [[roll-center]], [[camber-gain]]

**Physics.** The upper link's **angle** in side view (relative to the lower arm) sets roll centre and
camber gain on that corner. Two shim stacks set that angle — always judge them **net, together**:
- **Flatter** link (closer to parallel with the lower arm): **higher** upp

chunks.title: weight-distribution-and-ballast — Static weight distribution (front %)
chunks.excerpt:
**Keys:** `weight_balance_front_percent`, `total_weight` — front axle share of total weight, measured on scales in race trim.

**Founder-verified direction:** **more weight forward generally means less steering.** The heavier front reduces the car's **pendulum effect** — its willingness to swing into rotation — and the front tires carry more load than they can convert to extra grip (tire **load sensitivity**: grip rises **sub-linearly** with load, so overloading an end cost

chunks.title: weight-distribution-and-ballast — Ballast placement and polar moment (theory — not yet founder-verified)
chunks.excerpt:
Class rules set a **minimum total weight**; ballast is where you place the difference.

- **Low** placement lowers CoG → less load transfer everywhere → more usable grip. No real trade — always preferred.
- **Central** placement (near the CoG) minimizes **yaw inertia / polar moment** → the car starts and stops rotating more eagerly — quicker direction changes, livelier in chicanes, but less "flywheel" steadiness mid-corner.
- **Distributed toward the ends** raises polar m

chunks.title: weight-distribution-and-ballast — Left/right and lateral offsets (theory — not yet founder-verified)
chunks.excerpt: **Keys:** `motor_lateral_shift` — moving the heaviest components laterally trims **left/right balance**. On circuits with both corner directions, symmetric left/right weight is the standard goal so the car behaves the same both ways; a car consistently stronger in one corner direction is a hint to check lateral balance before reaching for chassis tuning. Battery/motor moves shift **both** lateral balance and front/rear split at once — re-scale after moving components.

chunks.title: bite-hold — Bite vs hold
chunks.excerpt:
*(driver-facing terms for what's canonically "initial vs overall grip"; the Engineer usually says
"bite / hold")*

**Feel — not physics.** Think of a grip curve: across the bottom is *how hard you're asking the
tyre* (how much you're leaning on it), up the side is grip.
- **Bite** (initial grip): the curve peaks **sooner, higher, and narrower**. Grip shows up fast and
  the ceiling is high — but the peak is a spike, and once you ask past it grip **drops away sharply**.

chunks.title: bump-compliance — Bump compliance
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre grips most consistently when the **vertical load** pressing it into the road stays
**steady**. A rough or bumpy surface throws that load up and down. The suspension can **absorb** those
inputs — the wheel moves, less reaches the chassis, the load stays steadier — or **pass them through**,
so the load spikes and drops and the tyre can skip or briefly go **light** (no load, no grip). How much
it absorbs is set by how freely the wheel can move for a road inpu

chunks.title: camber-gain — Camber gain (camber in roll)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Camber gain is how much **negative camber the wheel gains as the suspension compresses in
roll**. As the car leans in a corner the linkage tips the outside wheel to keep its contact patch
flatter to the road instead of rolling onto its outer edge. It's set by the **link and roll-centre
package on that end** — static camber (`camber_front` / `camber_rear`) only sets the starting angle,
not how much is gained.
- **Flatter** upper link → **less** camber gain.
- **Mo

chunks.title: camber-grip — Camber and grip
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre makes its best **lateral grip** at a certain **effective camber** (its static camber
plus [[camber-gain]] in roll) — enough tilt to keep the loaded contact patch working, not so much that
the patch shrinks. More camber builds peak lateral grip **up to that optimum**, then grip **falls off**,
often sharply; less camber gives a **lower peak** but a **more progressive** slip. A cambered tyre also
makes a little lateral force on its own (**camber thrust**) eve

chunks.title: damping — Damping
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A damper resists movement with a force that grows the **faster the suspension moves** —
near nothing at rest, more on a quick input or bump. So it doesn't set *where* the car sits (springs
do) — it sets **how fast** the car gets there: how quickly it rolls and pitches, and how sharply it
reacts to inputs and bumps. More damping → slower, more controlled movement; less → faster, more
reactive. Because it acts on rate, it governs the **speed of the elastic (spring)

chunks.title: differential-coupling — Differential coupling
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A differential lets the two **driven** wheels turn at **different speeds** — which they
must through a corner, since the outer wheel travels further. **Coupling** is how strongly the diff
**resists** that speed difference: **free** (open) at one extreme, fully **locked** (a spool — both
wheels forced to one speed) at the other. On power, more coupling drives the two wheels **more
together**, forcing the loaded outer and lighter inner toward the same speed against

chunks.title: load-transfer — Load transfer
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** In a corner, lateral g shifts vertical load from the inside tyres to the outside
tyres. The **total** amount is set by **CoG height, track width, and cornering g**. Most knobs only
change *how fast* and *where* it moves — but a few move the total itself: **track width**, and anything
that changes **CoG** (ride height, ballast, chassis).

Two facets the setup shapes:
- **Speed** — load reaches the outside tyres two ways: through the **links / geometry** (rol

chunks.title: motion-ratio — Motion ratio
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The ratio between how far the **wheel** moves and how far the **spring/damper** moves —
set by where the unit mounts on the arm. A unit mounted further inboard moves less than the wheel, so
its **effective rate at the wheel is lower** than its nominal rate. Motion ratio scales **both**
effective spring rate and effective damping — the same spring or oil gives a different wheel rate as
the mounting changes, and it can vary through the travel.

**Moved by:** spring

chunks.title: oil-viscosity-temperature — Oil viscosity vs temperature
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Oil thins as it heats and thickens as it cools — lower viscosity hot, higher
viscosity cold. So the same nominal oil gives **more damping when cold** (early in a run, cold
track) and **less as it warms**. A property of the fluid, independent of car or setup.

**Affects:** damper oil [[damper-oil]] (`damper_oil_front`, `damper_oil_rear`), diff oil
[[diff-and-driveline]], any silicone fluid.

chunks.title: on-in-track — On the track vs in the track
chunks.excerpt:
*(a subjective feel that refers directly to roll-centre height)*

**Feel — not physics.** Where the car carries itself, set by how high or low the roll centre is:
- **On the track** (higher RC): the car sits **up on** the surface — reactive, quick to roll, lively,
  and nervous if your inputs aren't smooth; you drive a little *within* the car.
- **In the track** (lower RC): the car sits **down in** the surface — planted, smoother, safer, easy to
  lean on with throttle. On **

chunks.title: roll-center — Roll centre
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** The roll centre (RC) is the geometric point the sprung mass rolls about in a corner,
fixed by the suspension-linkage pickup points (arm and link angles). Its **height** sets three things:
- **How much load transfers the fast, geometric way** — the higher the RC, the larger the fraction of
  lateral load that reaches the outside tyres through the links (near-instant) rather than through the
  springs (slow). It sets the fast fraction in [[load-transfer]].
- **Supp

chunks.title: roll-stiffness — Roll stiffness (elastic)
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** How strongly the car resists **body roll** through its **springs and anti-roll bars** —
the elastic path, as opposed to the geometry (that's [[roll-center]]). Springs resist both **heave**
(both wheels moving up together) and roll; an **ARB resists roll only** — it does nothing when both
wheels move together. It sets two things:
- **How much the car rolls** for a given cornering load (the elastic, slow path of [[load-transfer]]).
- **Front/rear split** — the bala

chunks.title: toe-and-scrub — Toe and scrub
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** Toe is how far a wheel points **in** (toe-in) or **out** (toe-out) of dead-ahead. A toed
wheel already runs a small **slip angle** going straight, so it makes a bit of side force before you
even steer — with **toe-in** the two wheels' forces point **toward** each other, with **toe-out**
**apart**; they cancel going straight but pre-load how the pair takes a set. That constant slip also
**scrubs** (drag, heat). More toe, more of both. Toe isn't only static: it shi

chunks.title: tyre-load-sensitivity — Tyre load sensitivity
chunks.excerpt:
**Physics.** A tyre makes more grip the more vertical load it carries — but **less than
proportionally**: double the load and you get less than double the grip; grip-per-unit-load falls as
load rises. So loading one tyre of a pair much harder than the other makes **less grip from the pair**
than sharing the load evenly would, all else equal.

A property of the tyre itself.
